scenes.title: Read the transition graph
scenes.objective: Refresh directed paths and transition probabilities.
body: A transition matrix can be viewed as a directed graph: draw i→j whenever pᵢⱼ>0.
State classification depends on which states can reach one another, whether a group can be left, and the possible return times.

items.ask: What does a directed path from i to j mean?
items.recall: There is a positive-probability route from i to j in some finite number of steps.
refresh: A directed path can contain one or several transitions. It exists when every edge on the route has positive probability; the product of those positive probabilities is then positive.
A direct arrow is sufficient but not necessary. For example, if 1 can move to 2 and 2 can move to 3, there is a two-step path from 1 to 3 even if p₁₃=0.

items.recall: i can reach j and j can reach i.
refresh: Communication is stronger than one-way reachability. State i communicates with j only when a path exists from i to j and another path exists from j to i.
If only one direction is possible, the states do not communicate. Mutual reachability groups states into communicating classes, which can then be checked for closure.

items.ask: What is the period based on?
items.recall: The gcd of all positive possible return times.
refresh: For state i, collect every positive integer n for which a return in exactly n steps is possible, equivalently pᵢᵢ⁽ⁿ⁾>0. The period is the greatest common divisor of this entire set.
The smallest return time alone is not enough. If returns are possible in 4 and 6 steps, the period is gcd(4,6)=2. A self-loop makes return in one step possible and therefore forces period one.

ask.q: What information do you need to classify states?
ask.nudge: Reachability, exits from classes and return-time possibilities.

scenes.title: A network of communicating states
body: In a directed network, two locations communicate if each can eventually reach the other. A one-way route does not establish communication.
A communicating class is closed if no transition from a state in the class leads outside it.

scenario.teaser: A one-way exit changes the class
scenario.title: A network with an absorbing destination
body: Consider three locations in a directed transition network. State 1 can move to state 2, and state 2 can move back to state 1, so the two states are mutually reachable and form one communicating class.
State 2 also has a positive-probability transition to state 3. State 3 is absorbing: once entered, the chain remains there forever. There is no path from state 3 back to either state 1 or state 2.

Consequently {1,2} is a communicating class but it is not closed, because a transition can leave it. The singleton {3} is a closed communicating class. In a finite chain, states in closed communicating classes are recurrent, while states outside all closed classes are transient.
scenario.answer: The singleton class {3}, because no transition leaves state 3.

ask.q: Why do states 1 and 2 not communicate with state 3?
ask.nudge: Can state 3 reach either of them?

blocks.body: i↔j if i is reachable from j and j is reachable from i.
Every finite closed communicating class is recurrent. In a finite chain, states outside the closed classes are transient. All states in a communicating class share the same period.

scenario.teaser: A finite chain has one exit from a communicating pair
scenario.title: Classify the transient states
body: A reliability network has two operating modes that can move back and forth, plus a terminal shutdown state. The operating modes communicate with each other, but one of them can send the system into shutdown.

Shutdown is absorbing: after entering it, the system cannot return to either operating mode. Thus the two operating modes form a communicating class that is not closed, whereas shutdown forms a closed singleton class.

To classify the states, do not simply ask whether they can reach one another. First form communicating classes using mutual reachability, then inspect every outgoing transition to decide whether each class is closed. In a finite chain this identifies the recurrent classes and the transient states.
scenario.answer: States 1 and 2, because they lie outside the only closed communicating class {3}.

scenes.title: Guided example: an alternating chain
scenes.objective: Compute the period from return times.
scenes.problem: A two-state chain has P=[[0,1],[1,0]]. Classify its communicating class and period.

steps.say: Each state reaches the other and returns.

steps.why: Both states remain in the class.

steps.say: State 1 returns only at even times.
steps.why: The period is the gcd of positive return times.

ask.q: Is this class recurrent even though it is periodic?
ask.nudge: A closed finite communicating class is recurrent; periodicity concerns the spacing of returns.

hints: Find the set of states reachable from each state and check mutual reachability.
Check whether any positive-probability transition leaves the proposed class.
Use the finite-chain result: states in closed communicating classes are recurrent; states outside them are transient.

solution.say: Each state reaches the other and returns.
State 1 returns only at even times.

scenes.answer: The two states form one closed communicating class. Both states are recurrent because the class is finite and closed, and each state has period 2 because returns occur only at even times.

scenes.title: Guided example: multiple closed classes
scenes.objective: Recognise transient states and multiple recurrent classes.
scenes.problem: A finite chain has two disjoint closed communicating classes C₁ and C₂. A state outside them can enter either class but cannot be reached from either. Classify the outside state and the two classes.

steps.say: The outside state can leave but cannot be revisited after entering a closed class.
steps.why: It lies outside every closed communicating class.

steps.say: Each closed class is recurrent in a finite chain.
steps.math: C₁ and C₂ are recurrent classes
steps.why: Finite closed communicating classes are recurrent.

steps.say: There is no single forced stationary distribution across the two closed classes.
steps.why: Stationary mass can be distributed between closed classes.

ask.q: Why is the outside state transient?
ask.nudge: Check whether the state can leave its communicating class and whether a return is possible.

hints: Identify the state outside C₁ and C₂.
Once it enters either closed class, can it return to the outside state?
Classify each closed communicating class and consider how stationary mass can be allocated between them.

solution.say: The outside state can leave but cannot be revisited after entering a closed class.
Each closed class is recurrent in a finite chain.
solution.math: C₁ and C₂ are recurrent classes

solution.say: There is no single forced stationary distribution across the two closed classes.

scenes.answer: The outside state is transient. C₁ and C₂ are separate closed recurrent classes. Stationary distributions can be formed by mixing the stationary distributions supported on the two closed classes, so the stationary distribution need not be unique.

scenes.title: Common classification traps
scenes.objective: Avoid one-way communication and period mistakes.

items.claim: If i can reach j but j cannot reach i, the two states communicate.
items.why: Communication requires reachability in both directions.

items.claim: A communicating class is closed only if no transition from any state in it leads outside the class.
items.why: Closure rules out every outgoing transition to an external state.

items.claim: A recurrent state may have period greater than one.
items.why: Periodicity describes the timing of returns; it does not imply transience.

ask.q: What quick test identifies an absorbing state's period?
ask.nudge: It returns at every positive integer time.

scenes.title: Exam summary
scenes.objective: Consolidate communication, closure, recurrence and period.
body: Communication is mutual reachability and partitions the state space into classes.
A class is closed when no transition leaves it. In a finite chain, closed communicating classes are recurrent; states outside them are transient.
Period is gcd{n≥1:pᵢᵢ⁽ⁿ⁾>0}. An absorbing state has period one; an alternating two-state chain has period two.

ask.nudge: Find classes, test closure, then classify recurrence and period.
